extracted.intended_audience: OMB/OIRA, Domestic Policy Council, federal regulatory agencies, and policymakers involved in regulatory cost-benefit and distributional analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies and OMB on how to identify, analyze, weigh, and mitigate distributional (equity) impacts of regulations, including methodological options (inequality metrics, social welfare function weights), interagency coordination, data collection, and systems-level oversight. Designed to inform rulemaking, OIRA review, and whole-of-government approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inequality metrics alongside disaggregated costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequality metrics should be considered as one set of available tools for agencies to incorporate distributional analysis into regulatory decisionmaking; using them alongside costs and benefits disaggregated by demographic groups may give regulators important information about how evenly costs and benefits are distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pending stakeholder input, present inequality metrics as a contextual data point to help regulators assess distributional effects alongside other regulatory impacts; use them to inform, not necessarily decide, policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Social Welfare Function (SWF)-based weights to disaggregated impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could assess distributional desirability by applying weights to costs and benefits based on a Social Welfare Function framework, which captures how social welfare changes with the distribution of utilities (well-being) in a population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SWF-based weights (typically income-based but possibly based on other well-being attributes like health) can be applied to disaggregated costs and benefits to rank policy options; OMB should consult stakeholders on whether income is the appropriate default and provide guidance if other attributes are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian weighting (income-based diminishing marginal utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilitarian weights translate income changes into utility changes by reflecting diminishing marginal utility of income (a dollar is more valuable to a low-income individual than to a high-income individual), giving greater weight to benefits accruing to lower-income groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilitarian weights can be extended to other well-being attributes but require measurement decisions (e.g., how to compare units of environmental quality). Because some attributes (race, gender, occupation) cannot be incorporated into a utilitarian SWF, agencies should present utilitarian-weighted results alongside traditional willingness-to-pay based CBA. Examples: UK Green Book provides specific income-quartile weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritarian weighting (priority to the worse-off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritarian weights assign higher value to well-being increments accruing to the worse-off than to identical impacts accruing to better-off individuals, integrating normative inequality-aversion judgments beyond marginal utility adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculating prioritarian weights requires normative parameter choices (aversion-to-inequality factors) that may be context-specific; empirical estimates can inform these parameters, but agencies would likely need to derive factors for each policy. Present prioritarian-weighted analyses alongside traditional analyses rather than as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present distributionally weighted CBA alongside traditional CBA (unless OMB prescribes otherwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighted cost-benefit analyses (utilitarian or prioritarian) should be presented as additional data points for decisionmakers, typically alongside traditional cost-benefit analysis rather than replacing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (e.g., Adler) recommend undertaking standard CBA alongside distributionally weighted CBA with a range of weights. If OMB permits weighted CBA as the primary result, it should give explicit guidance on defaults (e.g., income) and alternative well-being measures, and note limitations (e.g., inability of utilitarian weights to capture race).

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB should specify default measures and guidance if weighted CBA is used as primary
rubrics_metrics.description: If OMB endorses weighted cost-benefit analysis as the main decision tool, it should specify whether income will be the default measure of utility for weights and provide guidance for using other measures of well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit guidance should address measurement choices, comparability across attributes (health, leisure, environmental quality), and limitations; OMB should also weigh legal and practical considerations before adopting such a change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for legal and practical constraints of weighting approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying distributional weights is value-laden and may pose practical and legal challenges, including the risk that courts view heavily distributional justifications as outside agencies' statutory mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider whether they are empowered to make normative distributive choices, weigh judicial risk, and possibly limit weighted analyses to being informative rather than dispositive; OMB should recognize these tradeoffs when issuing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify adverse distributional outcomes during rulemaking and seek mitigation within authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should identify groups that will disproportionately bear regulatory costs or benefits and consider avenues within their statutory authority to address or minimize undesirable distributional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, lead agencies can design remedial measures (e.g., prioritize siting or programs to offset lost income) or coordinate with other agencies if mitigation is outside their authority; OMB can consult with agencies on rule-by-rule mitigation options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate interagency remedies when lead agency lacks authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If mitigating adverse distributional effects falls outside a lead agency’s statutory authority, the lead agency should work with other agencies to create remediation plans, with OMB or the DPC acting as a liaison or coordinator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include multiagency initiatives like the POWER Initiative or executive-order working groups; OMB/DPC could convene similar interagency groups to direct resources toward compensating adversely affected groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate pilot programs to study compensatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB and the DPC could initiate pilot programs to study and identify compensatory mechanisms (grantmaking, federal loans, technical assistance, procurement, financing) to address disproportionate harms from federal action or inaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot programs can gather stakeholder input and inform scalable remediation strategies for discrete disadvantaged populations (examples: coal communities, Cancer Alley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide systemwide oversight and data collection (OIRA role)
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA is well positioned to collect and oversee agencies’ distributional analyses, create centralized databases, and assess cumulative distributional effects across rules and agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA could set up an online database aggregating distributional effects by rule/agency/subpopulation, regularly review analyses to detect net effects on specific groups, and advise when distributional impacts merit corrective action analogous to its role on 'significant' rules under EO 12,866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the unified agenda and early flagging to surface distributional issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should flag potential adverse distributional outcomes early in the regulatory process, including preliminary distributional findings in semi-annual unified agenda submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early flagging enables OIRA to guide agencies through addressing distributional concerns during the rule development stage and facilitates stakeholder engagement ahead of notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA annual reporting on distributional outcomes to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA’s annual review and report to Congress could assess distributional outcomes (both for key rules and across rules) and report whether particular groups were adversely impacted by the year’s regulatory actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reporting provides a baseline for long-term assessment of regulatory equity and informs priorities for the following year’s regulatory agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate distributional measures into environmental justice or equity scorecards
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA could incorporate distributional issues into the environmental justice scorecard (per EO 14,008) or create separate scorecards to capture how well agencies are addressing equity in decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scorecards can help measure agency performance on equity and make distributional considerations more systematic and transparent across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an interagency working group to establish best practices and address methodological shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.description: An interagency working group on distributional impacts could identify methodological shortcomings, unquantified effects with equity implications, lead research, and produce best practices for distributional analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This group could partner with existing bodies (Equitable Data Working Group, Interagency Working Group on Social Cost of GHGs) to produce interoperable, systematic guidance, reducing the burden on individual agencies and enabling continuous improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt systems thinking for 'wicked problems' and distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat distributional issues as 'wicked problems' that arise from complex systems; systems thinking helps identify linkages, synergies, tradeoffs, and stakeholder perspectives across policy silos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many distributional harms are systemic and cross-cutting, agencies should consider whole-system effects rather than isolated rule-by-rule analyses; systems thinking supports multi-agency approaches and recognizes multiple possible solutions rather than a single fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct granular disaggregated analysis for a manageable set of subgroups and contextualize tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide guidance for agencies to conduct granular analysis that assesses costs and benefits for a manageable number of demographic subgroups and to weigh distributional concerns alongside other regulatory impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should include how to choose subgroup categories, how to contextualize magnitude/significance of distributional consequences, and how to balance distributional outcomes with other statutory regulatory objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit public input and establish stakeholder processes for whole-of-government equity implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of a whole-of-government approach to mitigating adverse distributional impacts should be informed by public input and robust stakeholder engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB/DPC should solicit public comment, stakeholder feedback, and input from affected communities to design coordination mechanisms, pilot programs, and methodological guidance.
